name: Esther Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy paper, cleaning products and bin liners for Danube Office Supply, which delivers to schools and small offices. Mornings are emails and price lists, afternoons are calls when a school's order is short. I came off the sales counter four years ago, so I'm still the new one on the buying team. I like finding a better price for a customer, and I hate the end-of-term rush when every school wants everything on one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing dramatic, and that's what I expected. At work I'd tell my team lead Brigitta that a bit of help with the dull emails is welcome, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little uneasy anyway, because Danube lost a big school contract in the spring and everyone's counting costs. Hype or not, a firm that is worried looks for savings, and the buying team is a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the chatbot to draft supplier emails, which saves me maybe half an hour a day. I'd put 100 pounds a month aside and keep an eye on the contract situation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady most of the time, with a small knot when the sales figures come out each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot now and then. What do you use it for today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to tidy up my wording when I write to a supplier who's let me down. I read everything before I send it, because it once invented a delivery date and I had a very embarrassing call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to the time it saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it spent on the customers, honestly. Ringing a head teacher who is stressed about toilet roll is the part that is actually worth my time. If the bosses just use it to cut the team, I'd be angry.

say: I'd tell my team lead Brigitta that **help** with dull emails is welcome.
I'd say it's good that nothing **dramatic** changes.
think: Danube lost a big school **contract**, so any worried firm looks at buying costs.
Hype or not, our small team is a **cost** to someone.
do: Keep using a chatbot to draft **supplier emails** and save about half an hour a day.
feel: **Steady** most days, with a knot when the monthly sales figures arrive.
S0.quote: Ringing a head teacher who is stressed about toilet roll is the part that is actually worth my time.
fieldNote: Already carries a **worry** about the lost school contract, separate from AI.
Uses a chatbot carefully after it once invented a **delivery date**.
Angry only at the thought of savings going to cuts, not to customers.

steps.text: Draft supplier emails with the chatbot and check every line
Move 100 pounds a month into the savings account
Keep phoning stressed school bursars myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm needs a plan before it needs a tool. At the union meeting I'd ask what happens to the people whose tasks get taken, because a promise of retraining is easy to say and hard to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is changing fast, and I'm the least experienced buyer on the team. Price comparing and re-ordering for regular customers is most of my week, and the software is already good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, not just for emails. I'd ask for a training day on the ordering software and offer to be the one who checks its suggestions. I'd also put my name down for any customer-care or account work that comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, though not frozen. I can see the road, and I think I can walk it if the firm lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of buying would you hand over first, and which would you never hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over the price comparing first, no sadness there. I'd never hand over the supplier who is late, because that takes judgment and a long memory of who keeps their word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the bosses if the team were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're the reason schools trust Danube, and that trust isn't in the software. I'd tell them to keep the people who talk to customers and to retrain the rest, and I'd say it politely, but I'd say it.

say: I'd say the firm needs a **plan** before a tool.
At the union meeting I'd ask what happens to people whose **tasks** are taken.
think: My job is changing fast and I'm the **least experienced** buyer.
Price comparing and re-ordering fill my week, and software already does them **well**.
do: Ask for a **training day** on the ordering software.
Offer to **check** the software's suggestions and apply for customer-care work.
feel: A bit **anxious**, though not frozen, because I can see a road.
S1.quote: I'd never hand over the supplier who is late, because that takes judgment and a long memory of who keeps their word.
fieldNote: Responds with a **practical** plan rather than denial or panic.
Locates her value in **relationships** and judgment calls.
Sees her junior status as the main **risk**.

steps.text: Ask Brigitta for a training day on the ordering software
Raise retraining promises at the next union meeting
Apply for the customer account role when it opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge thing and the government needs to act now, with rules and money. I'd write to my MP the first week, because waiting for the bosses to be kind is not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job probably goes within two years, and the firm will move fast because competitors will. Laszlo's bus pension will come in, but it's modest, so we'd be living on that and about four months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI every day to get as good as I can at it, so I'm useful until the end. I'd put every spare pound aside, tell our daughter Zsofi not to count on any help, and join the union's protest if they call one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, though I try to turn it into a list. Lists keep me calm, and I have a long one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your husband Laszlo retires in two years. How does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't change our plans for the house, which is paid off. What it changes is that his pension was supposed to be the extra. Now it might be the main income, and that's a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend those two years learning AI, or fighting for protection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly, but if I had to pick I'd pick the fighting. Learning AI helps me, but a rule that protects thousands of people matters more, and I can learn the tools in the evenings.

say: I'd say **government** must act now with rules and money.
I'd write to my MP in the **first week**.
think: My job probably goes within **two years**, because competitors will move fast.
Laszlo's modest bus pension would become our **main income**.
do: Use AI **every day** to stay useful until the end.
Put every spare pound aside and **join** the union's protest.
feel: **Frightened**, though I turn it into a long list to stay calm.
S2.quote: Learning AI helps me, but a rule that protects thousands of people matters more, and I can learn the tools in the evenings.
fieldNote: Splits effort between **self-help** and political pressure.
Her husband's pension turns from an extra into the **main** income.
Turns fear into lists; the **composure** hides real fear.

steps.text: Practise with AI tools every evening to stay useful
Save every spare pound toward living on the pension
Write to my MP about rules for AI at work
Join the union protest if they call one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people start now. I'd tell my colleagues to build their skills in the first year and not wait for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the same ending, only I'd be 63 and Laszlo would already be retired. I think I'd manage, but only if I use the time well and don't kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd go to evening classes in data and spreadsheets, and use AI for all my buying work. I'd try for the account manager job, then save hard so I can stop at 62 if it comes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two year one. I'd still lie awake sometimes, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years, practically, from the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a plan with a date on it, because dates stop me drifting. By year two I'd decide whether to stay at Danube or move to a school-supplies firm that still wants a human voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if the money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zsofi and my brother Peter, and the union, which has a hardship fund. I hate asking, but I've paid in for twenty years and that's what it's for.

say: I'd tell colleagues to build **skills** in the first year and not wait for the firm.
I'd say five years is enough if people **start now**.
think: The ending is the same, but I'd be **63** and Laszlo already retired.
I'll manage only if I use the time **well**.
do: Take **evening classes** in data and spreadsheets.
Try for the **account manager** job and save hard to stop at 62.
feel: Better than the two-year case, with a **plan** to hold onto.
S3.quote: I'd make a plan with a date on it, because dates stop me drifting.
fieldNote: Willing to take help from the union **hardship fund** she paid into for twenty years.
The extra time moves her from fear to **planning**.

steps.text: Enrol in evening classes in data and spreadsheets
Use AI for all my daily buying work
Apply for the account manager job at Danube
Save hard so I can stop work at 62

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway that nobody should panic. I'd also say that ten years is what we use for wars and pensions, so the government has no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 68, and I'd have retired before most of it lands. My worry shifts to Zsofi and her pupils, and to whether the pension is still worth what it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 65, use AI in my daily work as it gets better, and build savings up to about six months. Then I'd retire to look after our grandchildren if they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm for myself. A bit sad about the future the young people will meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, do you think you'd still be working when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not past 65, and I'd be happy with that. But I'd keep my skills fresh, because the pension can change and then I'd be glad I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Zsofi about her own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Zsofi to be a teacher who can do what a machine can't, and to keep her own savings. And I'd say vote, because the rules will decide how fair this is.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long runway, and the government has no excuse.
think: I'd be **68** and retired before most of it lands.
My worry moves to my daughter Zsofi, her pupils and the **pension**.
do: Keep working to **65** and use AI as it gets better.
Build savings to about **six months** before retiring.
feel: Fairly **calm** for myself, and a little sad for young people.
S4.quote: I'd tell my daughter Zsofi to be a teacher who can do what a machine can't, and to keep her own savings.
fieldNote: Calm about herself but her **concern** shifts to the next generation.
Treats voting as part of the **answer**.
Keeps skills fresh as insurance against pension changes.

steps.text: Keep working at Danube until I turn 65
Use new AI buying tools as soon as they're proven
Build savings to six months of expenses
Vote and write to my MP about fair pensions

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one worries me most, because Laszlo and I would be on his small pension with almost no cushion and I'd be too old to start again. What would help is rules that give people notice and paid retraining, and a union that fights for them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say older workers are slow with technology, and I'm not. I just want to see it work before I rely on it, and I've never been wrong waiting for that.

headlineQuote: I just want to see it work before I rely on it, and I've never been wrong waiting for that.
portrait: Esther is a **58-year-old** junior buyer at an office and school supplier, up from the sales counter.
Her husband Laszlo retires in two years, so her income and about **four months** of savings matter.
She is progressive and union-backed, and blames **rules** and employers more than the technology.
Steady and practical, she uses AI **now and then** and turns fear into lists and dates.
She moves from uneasy to anxious, and puts **retraining** and political pressure side by side.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with only Laszlo's modest pension and little cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Rules giving **notice** and paid retraining, and a union that fights for them.
